title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

reading.body:
This is a false positive in an automated licence-plate recognition system, occurring at the point where a machine-generated alert was passed to officers in the field for enforcement. The system matched a plate to a stolen-vehicle record on the basis of a single misread character, and the match was acted on as grounds for a felony stop. The failure sits at the handoff between detection and human action: the alert was treated as sufficient cause rather than as a lead requiring confirmation.

Catching this would have required verification of the hit before enforcement, which the vendor itself states should happen. The facts describe a misread character and a plate cover the sheriff's office called illegal, and they describe a stop carried out on the resulting alert. What is not established is whether any officer attempted to confirm the match before drawing a weapon, and the sheriff's characterisation of the deputy's conduct as reasonable is an institutional position rather than an independent finding.

The reporting rests on a single outlet, and the account of the cause comes from the sheriff's office. No court or outside reviewer has determined that the plate cover produced the misread, and no finding has been made on the detention itself.

reports.title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

summary: Steven Melvin, 42, of York County, South Carolina, was detained at gunpoint for over five minutes after a Flock Safety license-plate reader misread the first letter of his plate and matched his BMW to a similar stolen vehicle. The sheriff's office said an illegal tinted plate cover caused the malfunction and called the deputy's actions reasonable. Flock said alerts should be independently verified before enforcement.
title_en: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover
